children.text: The random forest from Chapter 3's case study passed walk-forward validation cleanly: a real, if modest, average edge, with a known, honestly reported instability across windows. The trader then builds a backtest of the actual trading strategy on top of it and reports a beautifully smooth equity curve with a Sharpe ratio above 2. That number looks like a completely different, much better result than the raw walk-forward accuracy would suggest, and that gap itself should be treated as a warning sign, not a reason to celebrate. Validating a model's accuracy and backtesting the strategy built on top of it are two different jobs, with two different sets of ways to fool yourself.

body.text: A model can pass every walk-forward check from Chapter 3 and still produce a misleading backtest, because backtesting a strategy introduces its own distinct pitfalls: execution timing that quietly assumes prices you could never have traded at, strategy rules tweaked repeatedly against the same historical data, and real market frictions, like circuit filters, that a clean spreadsheet calculation simply ignores.

children.text: The Look-Ahead Bias Hiding in Execution Timing

A signal computed using today's closing price cannot be filled at today's closing price. By the time that close is known, the trading session is already over. Yet a common backtesting mistake, easy to write by accident, multiplies a signal generated at today's close directly against today's own return, silently assuming a fill at a price that had already happened before the signal could have been acted on. The honest convention is to generate the signal using data through today's close, then simulate the fill starting from the next bar, typically the next day's open, or another realistically achievable price. This is the same look-ahead problem from Lesson 3, wearing a slightly different costume: using a price you would not actually have been able to trade at.

body.caption: A one-line mistake that back-dates a fill to an unreachable price
body.code:
# WRONG: multiplies today's signal by today's own return, a return that had
# already happened by the time the signal, based on today's close, existed
df["strategy_return_wrong"] = df["signal"] * df["ret_1d"]

# RIGHT: the signal is known only at today's close, so the earliest the trade
# could be filled is the NEXT bar; shift the signal forward by one period
df["strategy_return"] = df["signal"].shift(1) * df["ret_1d"]

children.text: Backtest Overfitting: Tweaking the Rules Until the Number Looks Good

Lesson 11 warned that trying 50 model architectures against the same validation window lets the winning architecture partly win by chance. The exact same risk applies once the model becomes a strategy. Tweaking the confidence threshold, the stop-loss percentage, or the position sizing rule, over and over, against the same historical backtest, until the Sharpe ratio finally looks good, is not strategy development. It is fitting the strategy's rules to the noise in one specific stretch of history, and it produces a backtest that looks excellent for reasons that have nothing to do with how the strategy will perform going forward.

body.text: If you find yourself running the same backtest dozens of times, each time nudging one parameter until the equity curve looks better, stop and ask whether you are validating a strategy or slowly hand-crafting a curve that fits one particular slice of history. The fix is the same one Chapter 3 relied on: check any promising rule change across several walk-forward windows, not just the one you happened to be staring at when it started looking good.

children.text: Ignoring Real Market Frictions: Circuit Filters and Halts

A backtest built on a clean price series quietly assumes you could always enter or exit at the price it computed. Real Indian markets do not always allow this. Individual stocks carry circuit filters, price bands, commonly 2, 5, 10, or 20 percent depending on the stock, and the Nifty and Sensex both trigger market-wide circuit breakers if either index moves 10, 15, or 20 percent in a session, halting trading nationwide, for 45 minutes at the 10 and 15 percent levels, and for the rest of the day at the 20 percent level. A backtest that assumes an exit was always possible ignores exactly the kind of tail-risk day Chapter 1's case study warned about, the same days a real trader might most urgently want to exit and might not be able to.

body.label: Market-wide circuit breaker halts (Nifty or Sensex move)
body.value: 10%: 45-min halt · 15%: 45-min halt · 20%: halted for the rest of the day
body.context: A backtest that assumes you can always exit a losing position on the worst days ignores this entirely. These are exactly the tail-risk days Chapter 1's case study warned about.

children.text: What a Trustworthy Backtest Report Actually Shows

markDefs.definition: The largest peak-to-trough decline a strategy's equity curve experiences over a given period, expressed as a percentage, describing the worst loss an investor in the strategy would have actually lived through.

children.text: Final cumulative return alone is not enough to judge a strategy. Two backtests can report the identical final return and describe completely different experiences to actually hold. A trustworthy backtest report always includes

, and a risk-adjusted return measure like the Sharpe ratio, alongside the headline return, because a strategy nobody could psychologically or practically have stuck with through its worst stretch is not a strategy you can actually run.

body.title: Spotting the fill-timing mistake
body.question: A backtest computes a signal using each day's closing price, then multiplies that same day's signal directly by that same day's return to calculate strategy P&L. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing, the signal and the return are from the same trading day so this is consistent

The signal, based on today's close, could not have been acted on until at least the next bar, so multiplying it by today's own return assumes a fill at a price that already happened before the signal existed
This only matters for intraday strategies, never for daily-frequency ones
The mistake is using closing prices instead of opening prices for the signal itself
body.explanation: By the time today's close, and therefore today's signal, is known, today's return has already fully happened. The trade can only realistically be filled starting from the next bar, so the signal must be shifted forward by at least one period before being multiplied against returns, exactly as shown in this lesson's code example.

body.title: The suspiciously perfect backtest
body.scenario: A researcher backtests a strategy and reports a Sharpe ratio of 2.3 and a maximum drawdown of only -4% over 3 years. When asked how the final stop-loss and position sizing rules were chosen, she explains she tried about 40 different combinations against this same 3-year backtest and kept the one with the best Sharpe ratio.
body.prompt: What is the most likely explanation for this suspiciously strong result, and what should be done before trusting it?
body.modelAnswer: Trying 40 rule combinations against the same 3-year backtest and keeping the best one is the strategy-level version of the hyperparameter search overfitting problem from Lesson 11. Some combination out of 40 was likely to look excellent on that specific 3-year stretch purely by chance, regardless of whether it reflects a genuinely robust strategy. Before trusting this result, the chosen rule combination should be tested on a separate walk-forward window, or several, that were not used at all during the 40-combination search, to see whether the strong Sharpe ratio and low drawdown hold up on data the tuning process never touched.

cards.definition: The assumption about when and at what price a signal could realistically have been executed; a signal based on today's close can only be filled from the next bar onward, never at today's own price.
Repeatedly tweaking a strategy's rules against the same historical backtest until performance looks good, fitting the rules to that specific stretch of history's noise.
A nationwide trading halt triggered when the Nifty or Sensex moves 10, 15, or 20 percent in a session, lasting 45 minutes at the two lower thresholds and for the rest of the day at the highest one.
The largest peak-to-trough decline a strategy's equity curve experiences over a given period, describing the worst loss an investor would have actually lived through.
A risk-adjusted return measure describing how much return a strategy generated per unit of volatility taken on, used alongside raw returns and drawdown to judge a backtest.

points: Validating a model's accuracy and backtesting the trading strategy built on it are two different jobs, and a strategy can look far better, or far worse, than its underlying model's validated accuracy would suggest, if the backtest itself is built carelessly.
A signal based on today's close can only be filled from the next bar onward; multiplying a signal directly against the same day's return is a common, easy-to-miss look-ahead mistake.

Tweaking strategy rules repeatedly against the same historical backtest is the strategy-level version of the hyperparameter search overfitting problem from Lesson 11, and needs the same fix: checking any promising change across multiple walk-forward windows.

Real Indian markets include circuit filters and market-wide circuit breakers that can halt trading entirely on the most volatile days. A backtest that assumes you could always exit ignores this real constraint.

A trustworthy backtest report always shows maximum drawdown and a risk-adjusted return measure like the Sharpe ratio alongside the headline return, since two strategies with the same final return can describe wildly different real experiences to actually hold.
